# Lab 7: Single-cell ATAC-seq analysis workflow

```{r include = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

## Notes

The estimated time for this lab is around 1h10.

This lab relies on the `fragments` file of a 10x Genomics scATAC-seq
experiment (~2 GB): its code is not run when the book is built, and no output
is shown on this page. Run it in your workshop session!

:::

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}

## Aims

- Import cells from human PBMC scATACseq dataset
- Perform scATACseq quality controls and checks
- Filter, normalize and plot PBMC scATACseq dataset
- Compute gene activity scores, check known markers and annotate scATAC clusters
- Perform differential peak accessibility analysis

:::

ATAC-seq data may be obtained in isolation using a single-cell ATAC-seq protocol
(e.g. [10X scATACseq](https://www.10xgenomics.com/products/single-cell-atac))
or in combination with gene expression data using a single-cell multiome
protocole (e.g. [10X multiome](https://www.10xgenomics.com/products/single-cell-multiome-atac-plus-gene-expression)
and [SHARE-seq](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33098772/)).

Several packages are currently avaialble to process scATAC-seq data in R. These
include [Signac](https://stuartlab.org/signac/) and
[ArchR](https://www.archrproject.com/bookdown/index.html). This lab will
closely follow the [processing steps](https://stuartlab.org/signac/articles/pbmc_vignette)
outlined in `Signac`, which interfaces well with `Seurat` for single-cell analysis.

In this lab, we will process a PBMC single-cell ATAC-seq (scATAC-seq) dataset
and perform preliminary analysis to assess quality of these data. The data for
this lab comes from [10X Genomics](https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/10-k-peripheral-blood-mononuclear-cells-pbm-cs-from-a-healthy-donor-1-standard-1-0-1).
The dataset contains roughly ~ 10,000 cells.

## Process human PBMC dataset

### Download data

The files we need are directly available from the 10x Genomics website. We 
download them in a `~/data/scATAC` folder (this may take a few minutes, the 
`fragments` file weighs ~2 GB). Note that the `fragments` file and its index 
(`.tbi`) must sit next to each other, with matching names. 

```{r filename = "R"}
scatac_dir <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "data", "scATAC")
dir.create(scatac_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
options(timeout = 3600)
url <- "https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/cell-atac/1.0.1/atac_v1_pbmc_10k/"
files <- c(
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_filtered_peak_bc_matrix.h5", 
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_peaks.bed", 
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_singlecell.csv", 
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_fragments.tsv.gz", 
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_fragments.tsv.gz.tbi"
)
for (f in files) {
    if (!file.exists(file.path(scatac_dir, f))) 
        download.file(paste0(url, f), destfile = file.path(scatac_dir, f))
}
list.files(scatac_dir)
h5_file <- file.path(scatac_dir, "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_filtered_peak_bc_matrix.h5")
peaks_file <- file.path(scatac_dir, "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_peaks.bed")
metadata_file <- file.path(scatac_dir, "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_singlecell.csv")
fragments_file <- file.path(scatac_dir, "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_fragments.tsv.gz")
```

### Import data

Notice how the count matrix is in a `.h5` format. We have already encountered
this kind of 10x Genomics outputs in [Lab 3](../day2/Lab3_Rbioc.qmd). Back
then, we imported them with `DropletUtils::read10xCounts`.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Does this function work here?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
scatac <- DropletUtils::read10xCounts(h5_file)
scatac
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

This works because 10X Genomics make sure to distribute files in `.h5` format
that are consistent accross single-cell sequencing methodologies.

However, the `SingleCellExperiment` obtained with this approach is not
the most convenient, as it cannot natively leverage `fragments` file (see below).

Instead, we can create a `Signac` object, a flavour of `Seurat` objects.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Import counts matrix and feature annotations using an import function provided by `Seurat`.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
library(Seurat)
library(Signac)
library(rtracklayer)
library(stringr)
cnts <- Read10X_h5(h5_file)
features <- import(peaks_file)
features$peak <- as.character(features) |> str_replace(':', '-')
metadata <- read.csv(
  file = metadata_file,
  header = TRUE,
  row.names = 1
)
```

:::
:::

How many accessible genomic segments were found in this dataset?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
features
length(features)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Create a `Seurat` object

The next step is to aggregate `counts` and `features` into a `ChromatinAssay`,
a scATAC-seq flavour of `Seurat` standard `Assays`.
The documentation for `?CreateChromatinAssay` indicates that the user can provide:

1. A `fragments` file, corresponding to the full list of all unique fragments mapped across all single cells.
2. Genomic annotations to the `ChromatinAssay`, corresponding to gene annotations,
promoter positions, etc. Such annotations can be generated from Ensembl.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Generate human annotations from Ensembl using a parsing function from `Signac`.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
## - Get human gene annotations (hg19/GRCh37) to feed it into the future `ChromatinAssay`
annotations <- GetGRangesFromEnsDb(ensdb = EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75::EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75)
GenomeInfoDb::seqlevelsStyle(annotations) <- 'UCSC'
GenomeInfoDb::genome(annotations) <- "hg19"
```

:::
:::

Create a `ChromatinAssay` using `counts`, `features`, `fragments` and `annotations`.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
## - Create Chromatin Assay
assay <- Signac::CreateChromatinAssay(
    counts = cnts,
    ranges = features,
    fragments = fragments_file,
    annotation = annotations,
    genome = "hg19",
    min.cells = 10,
    min.features = 10
)
assay
```

:::
:::

What are the dimensions of this object? Are they comparable to the count matrix? Comment.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
dim(cnts)
dim(assay)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

It's finally time to wrap the `ChromatinAssay` into a `Seurat` standard object!
This is done using the `CreateSeuratObject`.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Create a `Seurat` object from the `ChromatinAssay` object.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
## - Create Seurat object
PBMC <- Seurat::CreateSeuratObject(
    counts = assay,
    assay = 'ATAC',
    meta.data = metadata[metadata$is__cell_barcode == 1, ]
)
PBMC

PBMC[['ATAC']]
granges(PBMC)
Annotation(PBMC)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Check QCs

#### Cell-based QCs

The fraction of reads in peaks (FRiP) is a good indicator of how well each
cell was handled during scATACseq processing.

```{r filename = "R"}
PBMC$FRiP <- PBMC$peak_region_fragments / PBMC$passed_filters
PBMC$nCount_ATAC <- colSums(GetAssayData(PBMC, layer = "counts"))
PBMC$nFeature_ATAC <- colSums(GetAssayData(PBMC, layer = "counts") > 0)

quantile(PBMC$FRiP, seq(0, 1, 0.1))
quantile(PBMC$nCount_ATAC, seq(0, 1, 0.1))
quantile(PBMC$nFeature_ATAC, seq(0, 1, 0.1))
```

#### Peaks-based QCs

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Which analysis are the `fragments` required for, exactly?

Could we still perform normalization/clustering/annotation without them? And motif enrichment analysis?

Since we do have the `fragments` file at hand, most of the QC steps are
available (e.g. `TSSEnrichment`, `NucleosomeSignal` or fragment size distribution).
Let's go through them one by one.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
# compute nucleosome signal score per cell
PBMC <- NucleosomeSignal(object = PBMC)
PBMC

# compute TSS enrichment score per cell
PBMC <- Signac::TSSEnrichment(object = PBMC, fast = FALSE)
PBMC
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

The `TSSPlot` function from `Signac` can be used to plot the fragment count per
peak ~ TSS enrichment.

```{r filename = "R"}
PBMC$high.tss <- ifelse(PBMC$TSS.enrichment > 3.5, 'High', 'Low')
TSSPlot(PBMC, group.by = 'high.tss') + NoLegend()
PBMC$high.tss <- ifelse(PBMC$TSS.enrichment > 2.5, 'High', 'Low')
TSSPlot(PBMC, group.by = 'high.tss') + NoLegend()
```

The `FragmentHistogram` function from `Signac` can be used to plot the fragment
size distribution in peaks with different nucleosome signals.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Group genomic loci by their nucleosome signal (> 4 or < 4) and plot the fragment size distribution.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
PBMC$nucleosome_group <- ifelse(PBMC$nucleosome_signal > 4, 'NS > 4', 'NS < 4')
FragmentHistogram(object = PBMC, group.by = 'nucleosome_group')
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Filter cells and features

Just like standard scRNAseq data, scATACseq data needs to be filtered to remove
low-quality cells and peaks.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Filter the `Seurat` object (cells and features) as deemed appropriate.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
## - Filter data
PBMC <- subset(PBMC, subset = nCount_ATAC > 3000 & nCount_ATAC < 100000)
PBMC <- subset(PBMC, subset = nFeature_ATAC > 1000 & nFeature_ATAC < 20000)
PBMC <- subset(PBMC, subset = FRiP > 0.30)
PBMC <- subset(PBMC, subset = TSS.enrichment > 2.5 & nucleosome_signal < 4)
PBMC

## - Remove peaks with low coverage
PBMC <- PBMC[rowSums(GetAssayData(PBMC, layer = "counts")) > 10, ]
PBMC <- PBMC[rowSums(GetAssayData(PBMC, layer = "counts") > 0) > 10, ]
PBMC
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Dimensionality reduction and clustering

Now that the dataset is filtered, we can proceed to data normalization,
dimensionality reduction and clustering. Compared to scRNAseq, scATACseq data
is much sparser and has a higher dimensionality. This has important
implications for the choice of normalization and dimensionality reduction
methods. scATACseq data are generally normalized using a `TF-IDF`
normalization, which is implemented in the `RunTFIDF` function in `Signac`, and
dimensionality reduction is performed using `LSI` (Latent Semantic Indexing)
implemented in the `RunSVD` function.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Normalize then further reduce the dimensionality for visualization purposes.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
## - Normalize data
PBMC <- RunTFIDF(PBMC)

## - Reduce dimensionality
PBMC <- FindTopFeatures(PBMC, min.cutoff = 'q50')
PBMC <- RunSVD(PBMC)

## - The first LSI component is often correlated with sequencing depth
DepthCor(PBMC)

## - Embed in 2D UMAP
PBMC <- RunUMAP(object = PBMC, reduction = 'lsi', dims = 2:30)

## - Cluster cells
PBMC <- FindNeighbors(object = PBMC, reduction = 'lsi', dims = 2:30)
PBMC <- FindClusters(object = PBMC, verbose = FALSE, algorithm = 3)

## - Visualize data
DimPlot(PBMC, label = TRUE) + NoLegend()
```

:::
:::

What can you observe in the `UMAP` projection of the dataset? Comment on the
separation of some cell types into different spatially-resolved clusters.

:::
:::

## Compute gene activity scores

Signac's `GeneActivity()` function require scATACseq fragment information. Since
we have them, we can estimate a gene activity score for each gene in the `annotations`.

```{r filename = "R"}
gene.activities <- GeneActivity(PBMC)
```

We can now save this new object as an `Assay` in the `PBMC` object and normalize it.

```{r filename = "R"}
PBMC[['RNA']] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = gene.activities)

# - Normalize the new RNA assay.
PBMC <- NormalizeData(
    object = PBMC,
    assay = 'RNA',
    normalization.method = 'LogNormalize',
    scale.factor = median(PBMC$nCount_RNA)
)
PBMC
```

One can now visualize expression of individual markers across clusters to infer
cluster identity.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Assess the expression of known markers across clusters, projecting the cells in a 2D UMAP.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
DefaultAssay(PBMC) <- 'RNA'
VlnPlot(
  object = PBMC,
  features = c(
    'MS4A1', # B-cell
    'CD3D', # T-cell
    'NKG7', # NK cell
    'TREM1' # Monocytes
  )
)
FeaturePlot(
  object = PBMC,
  features = c('MS4A1', 'CD3D', 'NKG7', 'TREM1'),
  max.cutoff = 'q95'
)
```

Based on these markers, we can annotate clusters. **Note that the cluster
numbers obtained in your session may differ from the ones below**: adapt the
mapping to your own results!

```{r filename = "R"}
PBMC$annotation <- dplyr::case_when(
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(0, 5, 9, 12) ~ "Monocytes",
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 10) ~ "T-cells",
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(6) ~ "NK-cells",
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(8, 11) ~ "B-cells",
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(13, 14) ~ "DC"
)
DimPlot(PBMC, group.by = 'annotation', label = TRUE) + NoLegend()
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

## Find peaks differentially accessible across clusters

Finally, we can perform differential peak accessibility analysis to identify
peaks that are differentially accessible between clusters. This is done using
the `FindMarkers` function from `Seurat`, run on the `ATAC` assay.

```{r filename = "R"}
DefaultAssay(PBMC) <- 'ATAC'
Idents(PBMC) <- PBMC$annotation
da_peaks <- FindMarkers(
  object = PBMC,
  ident.1 = "Monocytes",
  ident.2 = "B-cells",
  test.use = 'LR',
  latent.vars = 'nCount_ATAC'
)
head(da_peaks)
VlnPlot(
  object = PBMC,
  features = rownames(da_peaks)[1],
  pt.size = 0.1,
  idents = c("Monocytes","B-cells")
)
CoveragePlot(
  object = PBMC,
  region = rownames(da_peaks)[1],
  extend.upstream = 10000,
  extend.downstream = 10000
)
```
